title: Migrating a large app to Swift 6
summary: Turn on strict concurrency module by module, starting with leaf modules, fix warnings, then switch the language mode. Treat it as a planned program, not a flag flip.
body: **In simple words:** Swift 6 mode turns data-race warnings into errors. In a big app that can mean thousands of errors, so you migrate gradually.

**Step by step:** (1) list modules and their dependencies; (2) in leaf modules (no dependents inside the app) enable complete concurrency checking as warnings; (3) fix them; (4) switch that module to Swift 6 mode; (5) move up the dependency graph; (6) track warning counts on a dashboard and block new warnings in CI.
**Swift 6.2 helps a lot:** `defaultIsolation(MainActor.self)` makes UI modules main-actor by default, so most code needs no annotations; only background work is marked `@concurrent`.

**Typical fixes:** mark UI types `@MainActor`; make models `Sendable` structs; turn shared mutable singletons into actors or protect them with `Mutex`; use `@preconcurrency import` for third-party code not yet updated.
**Risk control:** no behavior changes in the same PR, run tests with Thread Sanitizer, release with phased rollout, and watch crash rates (wrong isolation assumptions can show up as runtime traps).
**Staff angle:** write a migration guide with real examples from your codebase, provide templates and lint rules, hold office hours, and have a platform team own the hardest shared modules.
keyPoints: Migrate bottom-up: leaf modules first, warnings before errors.
Use default MainActor isolation for UI modules (Swift 6.2) to cut noise.
Common fixes: `@MainActor`, Sendable value types, actors/Mutex for shared state.
Measure progress (warnings per module) and prevent regressions in CI.
Roll out with phased release and monitor crashes.
mistakes: Flipping the whole app to Swift 6 in one PR.
Silencing errors with `@unchecked Sendable` or `nonisolated(unsafe)` without real protection.
followups: **How do you get 200 engineers to adopt it?** Clear guide, examples, lint rules, office hours, and a dashboard showing each team's progress.
**What breaks when async functions start running on the caller's actor?** Heavy work that used to run off main may now run on main; profile and mark it `@concurrent`.
